card lp-prod-heldout  [decided]
The held-out set
why: A builder optimises whatever it can see, so part of the merge bar has to stay out of its sight.
subtree: 7 cards, 1 open, 6 decided, 1 unchallenged

Builders never see this section. It runs every merge, inside the coordinator's loop, not once at the end.

Every line follows one path through the whole product, the way a user does. It never tests one part alone. Unit tests already check each part alone, and each part can pass alone. The bugs that remain are in the connections between parts, and a whole path is more difficult to fake than one function. #lp-split gives the reason this matters: a builder optimises whatever it can see, and an isolated feature is the cheapest thing to fake. #st-build-run is where this section runs: once per ticket merge, in the coordinator's loop, because the coordinator is a different agent working on a tree no single builder controls.

How a line is made: #lp-heldout-steps says what a line is, #lp-heldout-author writes the steps, #lp-heldout-binder turns them into tests, and #lp-heldout-feedback says what the builder gets when one fails.

  -> refines         lp-rubric-prod  The production rubric
  <- refines         lp-heldout-steps  A held-out line is Given/When/Then steps, not test code
  <- refines         lp-heldout-author  A step author writes the steps from the brief, in parallel with the builder
  <- refines         lp-heldout-binder  A binder agent turns steps into tests, and never makes a test pass
  <- refines         lp-heldout-feedback  On a held-out fail, the builder gets the text of the failed step
  <- depends_on      st-validate-heldout  The held-out set belongs to validate, and validate runs beside build
  <- refines         lp-heldout-mechanics  The builder never sees the held-out steps
  <- depends_on      werk-heldout-before-merge  The held-out set is built and gated on the run's tree before the merge loop runs it at each merge
  <- refines         st-heldout-step-fresh  A held-out step written before its source card changed is rewritten before it can file a follow-up

Keep it as its own card. Only the why is short. The card holds a whole mechanism:

1. Each steps file records the card versions its steps came from.
2. Before a run, a step whose card changed goes back to the step author, who rewrites it or drops it.
3. A step never files a follow-up while its card is newer than the step.
4. The card has a worked example, a picture, and two rejected options.

Folded into #lp-prod-heldout, this would be the biggest section of the parent. It would also lose its own options. Its siblings (#lp-heldout-author, #lp-heldout-binder, #lp-heldout-feedback) are separate cards for the same reason.

You are right that the parent does not mention the problem. #lp-prod-heldout says how a line is made and when it runs. It says nothing about a line going out of date. One sentence closes that gap:

> A line is a fair test only while the cards it came from read the same (#st-heldout-step-fresh).

Next: reply "add it" and I stage that sentence on #lp-prod-heldout as a proposal.

card st-heldout-step-fresh  [decided]

#st-heldout-step-fresh is now decided.

The contract check needs a kill criterion, so I recorded one:

- **What it measures:** follow-up tickets that stop at the retry cap while a red step contradicts a decided card. The data comes from the board log.
- **When it fires:** a count above 0 in 30 days, after at least 10 follow-up tickets.
- **What it falls back to:** `:opt0`, which checks each red step against the decided cards before the follow-up is filed.

If one such ticket still gets stuck, rewriting outdated steps is not enough. Then a check on each red step must also run.

The card has no stale mark. The new why that I staged earlier still waits for your ✓.
